questions.question: In a labor market, workers generally supply labor while
choices: households supply machines
employers demand labor
governments supply every job
firms demand finished consumer goods

questions.question: Why is the demand for labor called a derived demand?
choices: Workers demand employers because wages never change
Labor demand is set only by population size
Employers demand workers because labor helps produce goods or services people want
The demand comes from workers' personal spending

questions.question: What does human capital include?
choices: A firm's buildings and machinery only
Money held by a central bank
The number of products in a store
Workers' education, skills, experience, and knowledge

questions.question: If the demand for a firm's product rises, what may happen to its demand for workers?
choices: The firm may hire more workers to increase output
Labor demand must fall to zero
Worker productivity automatically decreases
The firm must reduce every wage

questions.question: A worker completes training that makes them more productive in a growing field. What may this increase?
choices: The number of hours in a workday
The worker's potential value to employers and earning opportunities
The price of every product in the economy
The firm's need for capital equipment

questions.question: At a particular wage, more workers want jobs than employers want to hire. This situation is a
choices: labor shortage
balanced labor market
labor surplus
shortage of consumer goods

questions.question: If employers cannot find enough qualified workers at current wages, the market may experience
choices: a labor surplus
a surplus of applicants
a fall in worker skills by definition
a labor shortage

questions.question: Which factor is most likely to shift the supply of workers in a particular occupation?
choices: Changes in training access or the number of qualified workers
A change in the firm's product price alone
A change in the employer's advertising budget
A change in the output of an unrelated industry

questions.question: An employer introduces technology that helps each employee produce more per hour. What may happen to the demand for labor?
choices: It must rise by exactly the technology's cost
It depends on whether the technology complements workers or replaces some tasks
It always disappears
It is no longer related to product demand

questions.question: Why can two workers in the same occupation receive different wages?
choices: All wages are legally identical within an occupation
Only the workers' job titles determine wages
Experience, location, responsibilities, skills, and employer conditions may differ
Wages never reflect productivity or labor supply

questions.question: A wage is the price paid for labor. In a competitive labor market, wages are influenced by
choices: the price of one unrelated product only
the number of firms' advertisements
the weather on payday
labor supply and labor demand

questions.question: A minimum wage set above the market-clearing wage may create a labor surplus in a basic supply-and-demand model because
choices: more people may seek work while employers demand fewer labor hours
all workers leave the labor force
employers demand unlimited workers
the labor supply curve shifts left by definition

questions.question: Why might a union negotiate wages and working conditions for its members?
choices: Unions set the prices of every consumer good
Collective bargaining can increase workers' negotiating power
Collective bargaining eliminates all workplace rules
Unions guarantee identical jobs for every member

questions.question: An employee receives a raise while their pay still buys fewer goods than before. What happened to the employee's real wage?
choices: It rose because nominal pay increased
It stayed fixed regardless of prices
It fell if prices rose faster than the employee's nominal pay
It cannot be compared with inflation

questions.question: Which situation is an example of occupational mobility?
choices: A worker changes the color of a uniform
A company moves its office to a different floor
A customer changes grocery stores
A worker retrains and moves from one kind of job to another

questions.question: A city has many job openings in health care but few trained applicants. Which response could help reduce the mismatch over time?
choices: Expand relevant training and credential pathways
Reduce information about job requirements
Discourage workers from gaining skills
Close programs that prepare qualified applicants

questions.question: What is the opportunity cost of choosing a full-time unpaid internship?
choices: The internship's posted job title
The income or other opportunities the person gives up
The total number of coworkers at the organization
The employer's advertising expense

questions.question: Why can wage differences across regions persist for the same occupation?
choices: Every region has identical employers and worker supply
Geography never affects labor markets
Local cost of living, labor demand, industry mix, and worker supply differ
Wages are unrelated to local conditions

questions.question: An employer compares two candidates with similar credentials. Which hiring practice is most appropriate?
choices: Select based on a protected trait unrelated to the work
Ignore the listed qualifications
Change the evaluation rules after seeing each candidate
Use job-related criteria consistently and avoid discrimination

questions.question: A worker's wage rises from $18 to $19 per hour while average prices rise 8% over the same period. What is the likely change in purchasing power?
choices: It decreases because the wage increase is smaller than the price increase
It increases because any nominal raise increases purchasing power
It stays exactly the same
It cannot change when wages rise
